S10281800108d.topic: A teaspoon of neutron star material would weigh roughly a billion tonnes on Earth.
S10281800108d.title: A Teaspoon of Neutron Star Weighs a Billion Tonnes #shorts
S10281800108d.description:
A neutron star is the collapsed core of a massive star. A teaspoon of its material would weigh roughly a billion tonnes on Earth. Follow for more weird science, explained calmly.

Narration uses an AI voice; visuals are AI-generated illustrations and royalty-free stock. Scripts are fact-checked, but if you spot a mistake, tell us in the comments.
S10281800108d.narration: A teaspoon of neutron star weighs about a billion tonnes. Let's unpack that. A neutron star is what's left when a massive star runs out of fuel and collapses. Its core crushes down until protons and electrons are squeezed into neutrons. Now picture about one and a half times the Sun's mass. Packed into a ball roughly 20 kilometers across. Roughly the size of a city. Your teaspoon of sugar weighs about five grams. This one weighs about two and a half times as much as all the people on Earth combined. Mount Everest, by comparison, is roughly 160 times heavier than that teaspoon. Some neutron stars spin hundreds of times a second. Wait, it gets weirder: they can sweep beams of radio waves like lighthouses. It's just matter squeezed beyond anything on Earth. Mind-bending, right? Follow for more weird science.

S102819104db3.topic: Daniel Kahneman's planning fallacy: we keep believing the next project will go faster than the last one, even when it never has.
S102819104db3.title: The Clockmaker Who Always Promises Friday #shorts
S102819104db3.description:
A quiet allegory about the planning fallacy, an idea Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky described in their research and that Kahneman explores in Thinking, Fast and Slow. Some other studies he cites there, such as priming and ego-depletion work, later failed to replicate, but the planning fallacy has held up well.

Narration uses an AI voice; visuals are AI-generated illustrations and royalty-free stock. Scripts are fact-checked, but if you spot a mistake, tell us in the comments.
S102819104db3.narration: In the town of Low Fen, the old clockmaker promises every clock will be finished by Friday. Every clock, every Friday, for forty years. Mist curls through her open window as she sketches tiny gears with quick, hopeful strokes. The last clock took three months, not three days. Her apprentice only smiles and pours the tea. She is certain this one will be different. Daniel Kahneman called this the planning fallacy: we keep believing our next task will go faster than the last, even when it never has. An idea from Thinking, Fast and Slow.

S10281910472e.topic: Daniel Kahneman: losing something tends to hurt about twice as much as gaining the same thing feels good (loss aversion; the exact ratio varies between studies).
S10281910472e.title: Why Humans Hoarded Dead Cables: Loss Aversion #shorts
S10281910472e.description:
Losses tend to feel about twice as strong as equal gains, a pattern called loss aversion, though the exact ratio varies between studies. Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky studied it, and Kahneman explains the idea in Thinking, Fast and Slow; some other effects he cites later failed to replicate. Thanks to Daniel Kahneman for the book this short is based on.

Narration uses an AI voice; visuals are AI-generated illustrations and royalty-free stock. Scripts are fact-checked, but if you spot a mistake, tell us in the comments.
S10281910472e.narration: Museum label, year 2126. Our ancestors refused to throw away a single sock. Why? Losing something tends to hurt roughly twice as much as gaining the same thing feels good. Find twenty dollars and enjoy it for a moment. Lose twenty dollars and it lingers all day. Specimens show drawers full of dead cables, unused gym passes, and cracked mugs kept just in case. Curators debate the exact ratio, since studies vary. The psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky named this loss aversion. Kahneman explored it in his book Thinking, Fast and Slow. Please keep your hands away from the sock.
